lead: Fresh fruit, vegetables, salad, herbs, mushrooms and sea vegetables as sold to eat, organised by crop group and species, then named cultivar, then origin (PDO/PGI/GI), club brand or breeder code, with marketing grades attached.

b.v: Extra Class > Class I > Class II
b.w: UNECE and EU marketing standards for fresh fruit and vegetables; the class is printed on the label or crate.

b.v: PDO / PGI / national GI
b.w: Fixes the growing area and sometimes the cultivar; a label of origin, not a grade.

b.v: cultivar or club brand named > generic
b.w: Flavour, texture and keeping quality follow the cultivar; club (managed) varieties are sold under a trade mark.

b.v: certified organic (EU leaf, USDA Organic, JAS)
b.w: Official organic schemes set the growing rules.

depts.t: Fruit of orchard, bush, cane and vine in cool and warm-temperate climates, sold by cultivar; sweet citrus → Citrus, warm-climate fruit → Tropical & subtropical fruit. Organic and fair-trade certifications are tags on a product, not kinds.
depts.ax: Is it a pome or stone fruit on a tree, a berry on a bush or cane, or a vine fruit?

b.v: U.S. Extra Fancy > U.S. Fancy > U.S. No. 1 (apples, pears); U.S. No. 1 > U.S. No. 2 for most fruit
b.w: USDA AMS grade standards for fresh fruit.

b.v: 特秀 (tokushū) > 秀 (shū) > 優 (yū) > 良 (ryō)
b.w: Grades used by Japanese co-operatives and gift-fruit shops for shape, colour and blemish (to verify).

b.v: measured Brix; tree- or vine-ripened > picked green
b.w: Premium fruit is graded and sometimes guaranteed by sugar content measured with optical sensors.

b.v: count per box or size code
b.w: Trade sizing printed on the box; bigger is not always better.

s.t: Tree fruit with a core of small seeds: apples, pears and their rarer relatives; stone-hard fruit such as cherries → Stone fruit.

ax: What part of which plant or fungus is it: a tree or vine fruit, citrus, a tropical fruit, an underground vegetable, a fruiting or pod vegetable, a leaf or stem, a salad leaf or herb, or a mushroom or seaweed?
key: 1. Is it a boxed or arranged gift of fruit? → Fruit gifts
2. Is it a mushroom, truffle or seaweed? → Mushrooms & sea vegetables
3. Is it a salad leaf, sprout or a herb used to flavour? → Salad & herbs
4. Is it a citrus fruit? → Citrus
5. Is it a sweet fruit from a warm climate (banana, mango, lychee, fig, date)? → Tropical & subtropical fruit
6. Is it a sweet fruit of orchard, bush, cane or vine, including melon? → Temperate fruit
7. Does it grow underground, or is it an onion, garlic or leek? → Roots, tubers & bulbs
8. Is it a tomato, pepper, gourd, bean, pea, sweetcorn, avocado or okra? → Fruiting vegetables & pods
9. Is it a cabbage-family crop, a cooked leaf, or a stem or shoot? → Brassicas, leaves & stems
Precedence: a salad radish is a root (step 7); an avocado, tomato and olive are eaten as vegetables (step 8) though botanically fruit; rhubarb is a stem (step 9) though cooked as fruit.
